---
title: "How to read your results"
description: >
  What each number in the output of fasttrop means, and what to do when
  fasttrop gives a warning message.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- The ATT is the mean effect of the treatment on all treated cells.
- The standard error and the interval come from a bootstrap. They are
  reliable only with many treated units.
- The tuning parameters show how much each of the three ideas of TROP counts
  in your data.
- Each warning message has a meaning and an action. The table at the end of
  this article gives both.
:::

## A fit to read

This article uses the example from the home page. It is a practice panel with
40 units and 20 periods. Eight units get the treatment in the last 5 periods,
and the true effect is 1 in each treated cell. By default, `trop_simulate()`
uses a hidden factor loading in the selection of the treated units. In this
panel, the treated units follow a hidden pattern more strongly than the
untreated units.

```{r fit}
library(fasttrop)
panel <- trop_simulate(n_units = 40, n_periods = 20, n_treated = 8, n_post = 5,
                       seed = 1)
fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            cv_cells = 200, n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
summary(fit)
```

The first lines of the output give the method, the design, and the size of
the panel. fasttrop finds the design from the treatment column. Make sure that
the design is the design that you expect. If it is not, examine the treatment
column of your data.

## The ATT

The ATT is the average treatment effect on the treated. It is the mean of the
effects for all treated cells, and each treated cell has the same weight. Thus,
a unit with more treated periods counts more in the ATT.

To get the effect for each treated cell, use `as.data.frame()`:

```{r cells}
effects <- as.data.frame(fit)
head(effects)
```

```{r cells-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.asp = 0.55, fig.cap = "The effect for each treated cell of the practice panel (grey dots), the mean for each period (teal line), and the ATT (coral line). The dashed line is the true effect of 1. The effects for single cells have much noise. The mean over many cells is more stable.", fig.alt = "A dot chart with the 5 treated periods on the horizontal axis. Each period has 8 grey dots, one for each treated unit, from approximately -0.5 to 4. A teal line connects the means for each period, which go from 0.3 to 2.3. A horizontal coral line shows the ATT of 1.22, and a dashed grey line shows the true effect of 1."}
by_period <- aggregate(tau ~ time, data = effects, FUN = mean)
set.seed(1)
ggplot(effects, aes(time, tau)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "22") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = coef(fit), colour = ft_col[["coral"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0),
             colour = ft_col[["grey"]], size = 2.4, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = by_period, colour = ft_col[["teal"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = by_period, colour = ft_col[["teal"]], size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = max(effects$time) + 0.15, y = coef(fit),
           label = sprintf("ATT = %.2f", coef(fit)), hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6,
           colour = ft_col[["coral"]], size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = max(effects$time) + 0.15, y = 1, label = "True effect = 1",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(effects$time)),
                     expand = expansion(add = c(0.3, 1.1))) +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Effect for the cell")
```

The effect for one cell is not a reliable estimate. Use the ATT, or the mean
over a group of cells, for example all treated cells in one period.

## The standard error and the interval

The standard error (SE) comes from a unit bootstrap. The resampling follows
Algorithm 3 of the paper. Each bootstrap draw takes a sample of units with
replacement. With the default `resample = "stratified"`, it takes the treated
units and the untreated units separately.

For each sample, fasttrop calculates the estimate again with the same tuning
parameters. The paper does not say whether to select them again in each draw.
The standard deviation of these estimates is the standard error.

```{r boot-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "The 200 bootstrap estimates of the practice panel. The coral line is the estimate. The teal lines are the limits of the 95% normal interval.", fig.alt = "A histogram of 200 bootstrap estimates. The peak is near the estimate. The right tail is long, and one draw is above 2. A coral vertical line marks the estimate. Two dashed teal vertical lines mark the lower and upper limits of the 95 percent interval."}
draws <- data.frame(draw = fit$boot$draws)
ggplot(draws, aes(draw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24, fill = ft_col[["teal_light"]], colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(fit$conf.low, fit$conf.high), colour = ft_col[["teal"]],
             linewidth = 1, linetype = "22") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(fit), colour = ft_col[["coral"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap estimate of the ATT", y = "Number of draws")
```

fasttrop has two types of interval:

- The normal interval is the default. It is the estimate plus and minus 1.96
  standard errors, for a 95% interval.
- The percentile interval uses the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws. To
  get it, set `ci = "percentile"`. This is the interval of the Python package
  from the authors.

In our simulations, the normal interval had a coverage nearer to 95%. With a
small number of draws, the percentile interval is less accurate. The article
[How we checked fasttrop](validation.html) gives the results.

::: {.limit-box}
Limits of the interval

- The paper says that the bootstrap is correct only with many treated units.
  For a panel with fewer than five treated units, fasttrop gives a warning
  message. Five or more treated units do not make the interval reliable.
- fasttrop keeps the tuning parameters fixed in the bootstrap. Thus, the
  interval does not include the variation that comes from the selection of
  the tuning parameters.
:::

## The tuning parameters

The line `lambda` gives the three tuning parameters. Each one controls one of
the three ideas of TROP:

| Parameter | What it controls | A value of 0 or `Inf` |
|---|---|---|
| `time` | How fast the time weights decrease with the distance from the treated period | 0 gives the same weight to all periods |
| `unit` | How fast the unit weights decrease when the history of a unit is different from the treated unit | 0 gives the same weight to all units |
| `nn` | The penalty on the low-rank term, which holds the hidden patterns | `Inf` removes the low-rank term |

With `time = 0`, `unit = 0`, and `nn = Inf`, TROP gives the same result as
TWFE imputation. This method fits two-way fixed effects (TWFE) to the
untreated cells only.

The line `Tuning` in the summary gives the criterion, the score of the
selected values, and the number of grid points that the search examined. A
smaller score is better. The element `fit$cv$trace` has the score of each grid
point that the search examined.

## A comparison with TWFE imputation

A fit with TWFE imputation shows how much the three ideas of TROP change the
result. To get this fit, set the tuning parameters to the TWFE values:

```{r twfe}
twfe <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
             lambda = c(time = 0, unit = 0, nn = Inf), n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
rbind(TROP = c(ATT = coef(fit), confint(fit)),
      `TWFE imputation` = c(ATT = coef(twfe), confint(twfe)))
```

In this practice panel, the ATT of TROP is `r round(coef(fit), 2)`, and the ATT
of TWFE imputation is `r round(coef(twfe), 2)`. The true effect is 1. Thus, the
estimate of TROP differs from the true effect by
`r round(abs(coef(fit) - 1), 2)`, and the estimate of TWFE imputation differs
by `r round(abs(coef(twfe) - 1), 2)`. One panel does not show the average bias
of either method.

The practice panel has a block design with no `NA` outcomes. Thus, the ATT
of TWFE imputation is also the treatment coefficient of a conventional TWFE
regression. In a staggered design, the two results can be different. The
article [How we checked fasttrop](validation.html) shows an example.

If the two results are very different, examine why. For example, the treated
units can have a different trend from the untreated units. In our simulation
B, TWFE imputation had a large bias in this case, and TROP also kept some
bias. The article [What TROP can and cannot do](limits.html) gives the
details.

## Warning messages and errors

fasttrop gives a warning message when you must use a result with care. The
table gives each message, its meaning, and the action to take.

| Text in the message | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Theorem 5.1 of the paper (triple robustness) has a proof only for a block design | The design is staggered or general. fasttrop calculates the estimate, but the triple robustness result has no proof for this design. | Report the design with the result. Do not use the triple robustness result as an argument for this design. |
| The treatment stops for some units | The design is general. The estimator assumes that the treatment has no effect after it stops. It also assumes that the effect does not change with the earlier treatment periods. | Make sure that these assumptions are reasonable for your data. |
| The bootstrap of Algorithm 3 is correct only with many treated units | The panel has fewer than five treated units. The standard error and the interval can be wrong. | Use the interval with care, and report the number of treated units. |
| The placebo cross-validation did not find a fixed point | The search for the tuning parameters of the global method stopped before the end. | Set a larger `max_cycles`, or set `lambda`. |
| The estimator did not use | For these treated cells, the weighted untreated cells cannot give the unit effect and the period effect. An example is a period in which all units are treated. | Make sure that each treated unit has untreated periods, and that each treated period has untreated units. |
| N fit(s) did not converge | The solver stopped at its maximum number of iterations. N is the number of fits. | Set a larger `max_iter` in `trop_control()`. |
| N of M bootstrap draws failed | Some bootstrap samples gave no estimate. The standard error and the interval use only the other draws. | Examine the panel for units with few untreated cells. |

Some errors stop the global method:

- The global method works only for a block design. For a staggered or a
  general design, use `method = "local"`.
- The global method must have at least two units that are never treated. With
  cross-validation, it must also have more units that are never treated than
  `placebo_size`.

## What to report

When you report a result from fasttrop, give these items:

- The method and the design.
- The ATT, the standard error, the type of interval, and the number of
  bootstrap draws.
- The tuning parameters, and how you selected them.
- The number of treated units and treated cells.
- The version of fasttrop. The function `packageVersion("fasttrop")` gives it.

Then write the result in plain words. For the practice panel, a report can
say: "The estimated average effect of the treatment on the treated units was
`r round(coef(fit), 2)`, with a 95% interval from
`r round(fit$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(fit$conf.high, 2)`." Also give the design
and any warning message. The interval shows the uncertainty of the estimate.
It does not prove that the treatment caused the change. That conclusion also
depends on the assumptions of the method.
